name: Sarguneswarar Temple, Tirukkaruvili Kottittai (Karuveli)
deity: Shiva as Sarguneswarar (Sarguna-Natheswarar), with the goddess Sarvangasundari (Sarvanga Nayaki)
period: Tevaram era (hymned 7th century); later Chola structural temple
summary: Karuveli, the Tevaram's Tirukkaruvili Kottittai, near Koonthalur in the Kaveri delta, honours Shiva as Sarguneswarar — the lord of all good qualities — with the goddess Sarvangasundari, 'the all-beautiful.' A Paadal Petra Sthalam hymned by Appar, it is remembered as the place where King Sargunan worshipped and won release from rebirth, and its very worship is held to bestow moksha.

sections.history: Karuveli, whose Tevaram name is Tirukkaruvili Kottittai, lies near Koonthalur in the Kaveri delta, about 22 km from Kumbakonam, close to the Thanjavur–Tiruvarur border (sources variously list Tiruvarur or Thanjavur district). It is a Paadal Petra Sthalam, hymned by Tirunavukkarasar (Appar). The village is also called Sarguneswarapuram, after King Sargunan who is said to have worshipped here and attained liberation. The stone temple is of the Chola period and later.
sections.architecture: A Dravidian delta temple, the shrine enshrines Sarguneswarar in the sanctum, with the goddess Sarvangasundari — also Sarvanga Nayaki — in her own shrine, her standing image remarkable at some five and a half feet tall. A Nandi and the parivara devatas complete the plan. The sacred tank, the Yama Theertham, lies outside the temple; its name recalls the lord's power over death and the moksha sought here.
sections.legends: The lord's name Sarguneswarar means 'the lord of all good qualities' (sarva-guna), and the goddess Sarvangasundari is 'she who is beautiful in every limb.' The sthala legend tells of a king named Sargunan who worshipped Shiva here with such devotion that he was freed from the cycle of birth and death, giving the village the name Sarguneswarapuram. The Yama Theertham, named for the lord of death, marks the place as one where the fear of death is overcome and moksha granted.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps Maha Shivaratri in Masi (February–March), Navaratri in Purattasi (September–October) and the Mondays of Karthikai, with Pradosha worship. As a shrine famed for granting moksha, it draws devotees who seek release, especially on Shivaratri nights.
sections.experience: Karuveli offers the pilgrim a shrine whose whole promise is liberation. Before Sarguneswarar and the tall, serene form of Sarvangasundari, beside the Yama Theertham that recalls the conquest of death, the visitor stands where a king is said to have won release — a quiet delta temple whose name and legend hold out the hope of moksha.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Karuveli is about 22 km from Kumbakonam, reached via the Kumbakonam–Natchiarkoil–Poonthottam road to Koonthalur, then north across the Arasalaru about 2 km to the temple (Koondhalur post, near the Thanjavur–Tiruvarur border). Kumbakonam is the nearest major rail head, with buses toward Koonthalur and local taxis.
